front: {{c1::Absolute}} deprivation is lacking the resources for survival; {{c2::relative}} deprivation is perceiving less than a reference group believes it deserves.
why: Relative deprivation is commonly tested via social movements

front: {{c1::Absolute}} poverty is lacking basic survival needs (food, shelter); {{c2::relative}} poverty is deprivation compared to one's society's standards.
why: Absolute vs relative poverty is named on 10A and tested every year

front: {{c1::Cultural capital}} (Bourdieu): nonfinancial assets — tastes, manners, credentials, speech — conferring status advantage, transmitted by family and school.
why: Cultural capital is tested on essentially every administration

front: {{c1::De jure}} segregation is imposed by law; {{c2::de facto}} segregation persists in practice through housing markets, lending, and school assignment.
why: De jure/de facto segregation supports residential segregation content

front: {{c1::Horizontal}} mobility is movement between positions of roughly equal rank, e.g., a nurse becoming a respiratory therapist.
why: Restates the vertical vs horizontal mobility card; keep the fuller contrast

front: {{c1::Institutional}} discrimination yields unequal outcomes through policy, not prejudice; {{c2::individual}} discrimination is one person's act.
why: Individual vs institutional discrimination is tested every year

front: {{c1::Intergenerational}} mobility compares your class position to your parents'; {{c2::intragenerational}} mobility is movement within your own lifetime.
why: Intergenerational vs intragenerational mobility is tested every year

front: {{c1::Intersectionality}} (Crenshaw): race, class, and gender form interlocking systems of disadvantage that cannot be understood one axis at a time.
why: Intersectionality is a named concept tested every administration

front: {{c1::Mills}}'s power elite thesis says a small corporate, military, and political network makes key decisions; {{c2::pluralism}} says power is dispersed.
why: Power elite vs pluralism is second-tier theory

front: {{c1::Race}} is a socially assigned category based on perceived physical traits; {{c2::ethnicity}} is shared culture, ancestry, and language.
why: Race as social construct vs ethnicity is tested every year

front: {{c1::Social capital}} is advantage derived from networks and connections — who you know and the resources those ties can mobilize.
why: Social capital is AAMC-listed and tested every administration

front: {{c1::Social reproduction}} is the transmission of class position across generations via schooling, cultural capital, and inherited wealth.
why: Social reproduction is AAMC-listed; commonly tested

front: {{c1::Structural}} mobility comes from economy-wide change — factory automation, tech booms — moving whole groups regardless of individual effort.
why: Structural mobility is a commonly tested mobility pattern

front: {{c1::World-systems}} theory (Wallerstein): core nations extract profit from periphery nations, with a semi-periphery in between.
why: World-systems core/periphery is the standard global-inequality item

front: A {{c1::caste}} system is closed — status ascribed at birth, endogamy enforced, no mobility; a {{c2::class}} system is open, mixing ascription with achievement.
why: Caste vs class (closed vs open) is core stratification, tested every year

front: A reference group is one that:
why: Reference group is commonly tested; also carded in the groups deck

front: A surgeon's son becomes a struggling artist. Classify the mobility.
why: Classifying mobility from a scenario is how mobility gets tested

front: Automation eliminates factory jobs and forces many workers into service work. Is this exchange mobility or structural mobility?
why: Structural vs exchange mobility applied to a scenario; common stem

front: Beyond income, which markers do sociologists use to place a household in a social class?
why: How class is placed beyond SES components is supporting detail

front: Bourdieu's {{c1::habitus}} is the durable set of dispositions, tastes, and bodily habits instilled by one's class position and carried into every setting.
why: Habitus is not on the AAMC outline; cultural capital card covers the mechanism

front: Compare the three major sociological perspectives.
why: The three perspectives are the foundation of 9A, tested every year

front: Contrast absolute and relative poverty.
why: Restates the absolute/relative poverty cloze card in the same deck

front: Contrast class, caste, and meritocracy systems.
why: Adds meritocracy to the caste/class contrast already covered

front: Contrast modernization theory and dependency theory of global inequality.
why: Modernization vs dependency is second-tier global inequality theory

front: Davis and Moore argued that stratification is functional. State their claim and Tumin's central criticism.
why: Davis-Moore is prep-book standard; Tumin critique is detail

front: Define ascribed vs. achieved status, and master status.
why: Ascribed/achieved/master status is tested every administration

front: Distinguish class consciousness from false consciousness (Marx).
why: Class vs false consciousness is AAMC-listed; commonly tested

front: Distinguish role strain from role conflict.
why: Role strain vs role conflict is tested every year

front: Distinguish vertical from horizontal social mobility with examples.
why: Vertical vs horizontal mobility is on the outline; commonly tested

front: Education is the strongest individual lever for upward mobility, yet US mobility trails much of Europe. Reconcile these two facts.
why: US-vs-Europe mobility essay; opportunity hoarding detail not on outline

front: How can relative poverty damage health even in wealthy nations?
why: Links relative poverty to health; Wilkinson is flavor

front: How does cultural capital shape medical school admissions?
why: Application restating the cultural capital card

front: How does intersectionality explain the pay gap for Black women?
why: Applies intersectionality; the definition card carries the point

front: How does the social model of disability differ from the medical model?
why: Medical vs social model of disability is commonly tested

front: How is occupational prestige measured, and what pattern emerges?
why: How prestige surveys are conducted is measurement trivia

front: How would Weber analyze a lottery winner who is snubbed by old-money elites?
why: Restates the status inconsistency cloze card

front: Identical resumes with white-sounding names drew about 50 percent more callbacks than those with Black-sounding names. Why is this design strong evidence?
why: Named audit study; the design point is research methods, not stratification

front: In world-systems terms, classify Germany, Brazil, and a raw-material-exporting low-income nation.
why: Restates the world-systems card with country examples

front: Manifest vs. latent functions are:
why: Manifest vs latent function is tested every administration

front: Marx: the {{c1::bourgeoisie}} own the means of production; the {{c2::proletariat}} sell labor power; their conflict drives historical change.
why: Marx bourgeoisie/proletariat is core conflict theory, tested every year

front: SES is conventionally measured by three components: {{c1::income}}, {{c2::education}}, and occupational prestige.
why: SES components (income, education, occupation) are tested every year

front: The {{c1::feminization of poverty}}: women — especially single mothers and elderly women — are disproportionately represented among the poor.
why: Feminization of poverty is a named, commonly tested pattern

front: The {{c1::Gini coefficient}} summarizes income inequality from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything).
why: Gini coefficient is plausible passage data; values are trivia

front: The {{c1::glass ceiling}} blocks promotion to top positions; the {{c2::glass escalator}} speeds men upward in female-dominated fields such as nursing.
why: Glass ceiling/escalator are commonly tested gender-stratification terms

front: The sick role (Parsons) includes the obligation to:
why: Parsons' sick role obligations are tested every administration

front: Weber applied: a professor is high in {{c1::prestige}} but modest in property; a kingpin is rich but scorned — {{c2::status inconsistency}}.
why: Status inconsistency illustrates Weber's dimensions; second step

front: Weber's {{c1::life chances}} are the opportunities to obtain valued goods, including {{c2::health}} and longevity, determined largely by market position.
why: Life chances ties class to health; supporting Weber vocabulary

front: Weber's three components of stratification are {{c1::class, status, and party (power)}}.
why: Weber's class/status/party is core stratification theory; commonly tested

front: What are the core principles of social stratification as a concept?
why: Textbook list of stratification principles; no reasoning payoff

front: What are the principal systems of stratification across history?
why: Slavery/caste/estate/class survey is second-tier

front: What does social reproduction mean?
why: Restates the social reproduction cloze card

front: What is a status group in Weber's sense, and how does it differ from class?
why: Restates Weber's status dimension already covered by two cards

front: What is an official poverty line, and what are its main critiques?
why: US poverty-line history and critiques are policy minutiae

front: What is intersectionality?
why: Restates the intersectionality cloze card

front: What is opportunity hoarding, and how does it undercut meritocracy claims?
why: Opportunity hoarding is not on the AAMC outline

front: What is social capital?
why: Restates the social capital cloze card

front: What is social exclusion?
why: Social exclusion is named on 10A under poverty

front: What is the 'culture of poverty' thesis, and why is it criticized?
why: Culture of poverty is prep-book standard; critique is context

front: What is the meritocracy paradox in education?
why: Meritocracy as ideology is a plausible but secondary frame

front: What mechanisms keep caste systems closed?
why: Mechanisms of caste closure are detail beyond the caste/class contrast

front: Which of the following best describes cultural transmission?
why: Cultural transmission is commonly tested, though a culture-topic card

front: Which sociological perspective views society as interdependent parts serving functions?
why: Restates the three-perspectives card

front: Why can a numerical majority still be a sociological minority group?
why: Minority group defined by power not headcount is a common stem

front: Why do sociologists prefer the Human Development Index to GDP per capita when comparing countries?
why: HDI vs GDP is not on the AAMC outline

front: Why do wealth gaps exceed income gaps, and why does the distinction matter?
why: Wealth vs income gap is plausible passage reasoning

front: Why does the Black-white wealth gap remain far larger than the income gap even among households with equal education?
why: Restates the wealth-vs-income card with US policy history

front: Why was apartheid South Africa described as a caste-like system?
why: Restates the caste card's apartheid example

front: William Julius Wilson linked deindustrialization and out-migration to concentrated inner-city poverty. Name the two mechanisms he emphasized.
why: Named scholar's specific mechanisms; trivia-grade

front: World systems theory divides nations into:
why: Restates the world-systems cloze card
